title: Every matrix rotates, stretches, rotates
objectives: Find singular values from the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.
Tell singular values apart from eigenvalues.

screens.title: Stretch the circle
screens.prose: The matrix $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ sends each point $\mathbf{x}$ on the unit circle to $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$. Drag $\mathbf{x}$ round the circle and watch the length of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$.
screens.question: What is the largest length $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}|$ you can reach?

widget.accept: 4, reached at $\mathbf{x} = (0.89, 0.45)$. Answers from 3.97 to 4.03 are accepted.
widget.label: Largest length

hints.text: Try directions between the two axes, not only the axes themselves.
The arrow $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is longest when it points at the far end of the tilted ellipse.
Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to about 27° above the positive $x$-axis and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep dragging and read the largest value the caption shows.

byKey.start: 3.61 is the length at the starting point, $\mathbf{x} = (1, 0)$. Drag further round: a direction between the axes does better.
byKey.eigen: 2 is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$, but no direction you drag stops at 2 as the longest. Drag and read the caption.

explain.text: You found the longest image, length 4, at $\mathbf{x} = (0.89, 0.45)$, about 27° above the axis. Every point of the circle lands on the tilted ellipse. That direction lands on its far end.

screens.prose: That longest stretch, 4, is the first **singular value** of $\mathbf{A}$, written $\sigma_1$. The direction that reaches it is $\mathbf{v}_1 = (0.89, 0.45)$. Now look for the shortest image.
screens.question: What is the smallest length $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}|$ you can reach?

widget.accept: 1, reached at $\mathbf{x} = (-0.45, 0.89)$. Answers from 0.97 to 1.03 are accepted.
widget.label: Smallest length

hints.text: The shortest image points at the nearest part of the ellipse.
Try the direction at right angles to $\mathbf{v}_1$.
Drag $\mathbf{x}$ to about 117°, up and to the left, and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag until the caption shows its smallest value.

byKey.eigen: 2 is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$. One direction is squeezed below that: drag and read the caption.
byKey.zero: No point of the circle is sent to the origin: $\mathbf{A}$ is invertible. Read the smallest length the caption shows.

explain.text: You found length 1 at $\mathbf{x} = (-0.45, 0.89)$, at right angles to $\mathbf{v}_1$. So $\sigma_2 = 1$ and that direction is $\mathbf{v}_2$. The ellipse's semi-axes have lengths $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 = 1$.

screens.title: Three moves
screens.prose: $\mathbf{A}$ can be done as three simple moves in turn. Slide the stage from 0 to 3. Watch the circle and the two directions $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ you found.

derive.V1.label: s > 2.98 ? '$4\\mathbf{u}_1$' : '$\\mathbf{v}_1$'
derive.V2.label: s > 2.98 ? '$\\mathbf{u}_2$' : '$\\mathbf{v}_2$'
derive.caption: {{s < 0.02 ? 'Start: the unit circle and two directions' : s < 1.001 ? 'Stage 1: turn by −27°' : s < 2.001 ? 'Stage 2: stretch along the axes, by 4 and by 1' : 'Stage 3: turn by +63°'}}

screens.question: Which stage changes the shape of the circle?

options.why: During stage 1 the circle only turns. It is still a circle, and only the arrows move.
Stage 3 turns the ellipse but keeps its shape. Slide back to stage 2 to see where the shape changes.
Slide through stages 1 and 3 again. A turn moves the arrows but leaves the shape alone.

feedback.correct: Only the stretch changes the shape.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide one stage at a time and watch the outline, not the arrows.

explain.text: Stage 1 turns the plane so $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ lie on the axes. Stage 2 stretches along the axes, by 4 and by 1, and only this changes the shape. Stage 3 turns the ellipse into its final place.

screens.prose: Each stage is a matrix. Stage 1 is a rotation $\mathbf{V}^T$, stage 2 a stretch $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ along the axes, stage 3 a rotation $\mathbf{U}$. Here $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the stretch matrix, not a covariance. The slider starts at the end of stage 1.

derive.V1.label: s > 2.98 ? '$4\\mathbf{u}_1$' : '$\\mathbf{v}_1$'
derive.V2.label: s > 2.98 ? '$\\mathbf{u}_2$' : '$\\mathbf{v}_2$'
derive.caption: {{s < 0.02 ? 'Start: the unit circle and two directions' : s < 1.001 ? 'Stage 1: turn by −27°' : s < 2.001 ? 'Stage 2: stretch along the axes, by 4 and by 1' : 'Stage 3: turn by +63°'}}

screens.question: Where is $\mathbf{v}_1$ at the end of stage 1?

options.why: That is where $\mathbf{v}_2$ goes. $\mathbf{v}_1$ is the long direction, so it goes to the axis that stage 2 stretches by 4.
Stage 1 turns every vector by −27°, so $\mathbf{v}_1$ moves. Look at the arrow at stage 1.
That is after stage 2 as well. A rotation keeps lengths, so after stage 1 the arrow still has length 1.

hints.text: A rotation keeps lengths. How long is the arrow after stage 1?
Look at the arrow for $\mathbf{v}_1$ when the slider reads 1.
$\mathbf{V}^T$ turns $\mathbf{v}_1$ by −27°, from 27° down to 0°. It lands on the positive $x$-axis with length 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the arrow at the end of stage 1, and remember a turn keeps lengths.

explain.text: $\mathbf{V}^T$ turns $\mathbf{v}_1$ onto $(1, 0)$. Then $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ makes it $(4, 0)$, and $\mathbf{U}$ turns it to $4\mathbf{u}_1$. So $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1 = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1$: each input direction lands on an axis of the ellipse.

screens.title: Stretches without dragging
screens.prose: To compute the stretches, square them: $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}|^2 = (\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x})^T(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x}$. So everything depends on the symmetric matrix $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

hints.text: Entry $(i, j)$ of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is column $i$ of $\mathbf{A}$ dotted with column $j$.
The columns of $\mathbf{A}$ are $(2, 3)$ and $(0, 2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each column of $\mathbf{A}$ with each column.

byKey.r1c1: The matrix is symmetric, so row 2, column 1 matches row 1, column 2.

explain.text: Each entry is a dot product of two columns of $\mathbf{A}$. The result is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are perpendicular. Those eigenvectors will be the directions you dragged to.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalues 16 and 1. Its eigenvectors are $(0.89, 0.45)$ and $(-0.45, 0.89)$: exactly the directions $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ you dragged to.
screens.question: What are the singular values $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ of $\mathbf{A}$?

options.why: You took the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. They are squared lengths, since $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}|^2 = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$. Take square roots.
Those are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ itself, read off its diagonal. Singular values come from $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.
You read the diagonal of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. Its eigenvalues are 16 and 1, not its diagonal entries.

hints.text: Put $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{v}_1$ into $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}|^2 = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$.
$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1 = 16\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_1^T\mathbf{v}_1 = 1$.
$|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1|^2 = 16$, so $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1| = 4$. Likewise $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_2| = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ are squared stretches.

explain.text: $|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1|^2 = \mathbf{v}_1^T(16\mathbf{v}_1) = 16$, so $\sigma_1 = 4$, the length you dragged to. Likewise $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{1} = 1$. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

screens.title: Not square
screens.prose: $\mathbf{B}$ sends 3-d vectors to the plane, so it has no eigenvalues at all. It still has singular values. $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^T$ has eigenvalues 3 and 1, and $\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{B}$ has 3, 1 and 0.
screens.question: What is the largest singular value $\sigma_1$ of $\mathbf{B}$?

hints.text: Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues, as before.
The largest eigenvalue on offer is 3.
$\sigma_1 = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732$, and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{1} = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of the largest eigenvalue.

byKey.noroot: 3 is the eigenvalue, a squared stretch. Take its square root.
byKey.zero: 0 is the extra eigenvalue of the 3 by 3 matrix $\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{B}$: a direction $\mathbf{B}$ sends to zero. Ask for the largest instead.
byKey.two: 2 is a diagonal entry of $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^T$, not an eigenvalue. Use the eigenvalue 3.

explain.text: $\sigma_1 = \sqrt3$ and $\sigma_2 = 1$. The two products share their non-zero eigenvalues: if $\mathbf{B}^T\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ then $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^T(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v}) = \lambda(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{v})$. So every matrix, square or not, has singular values.

screens.title: Eigenvalues are not stretches
screens.prose: The shear $\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 1 and 1. A colleague concludes it stretches nothing.

state.caption: The unit circle (dashed) and its image under the shear

screens.question: What is the largest singular value of $\mathbf{S}$?

options.why: You used the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{S}$. They describe only the direction $(1, 0)$, which keeps its line. The ellipse reaches well past the circle elsewhere.
2.618 is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{S}$, a squared stretch. Take its square root.
You added the entries of a row. The stretch comes from the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{S}$.

hints.text: Is the dashed circle the same size as the ellipse?
Singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{S}$.
$\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 2.618 and 0.382. Take square roots: 1.618 and 0.618.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take square roots of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{S}$.

byKey.one: You used the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{S}$. They only say $(1, 0)$ keeps its line and its length. Other directions stretch by up to 1.618.

explain.text: The ellipse reaches 1.618 from the centre in direction $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{v}_1$, with $\mathbf{v}_1 = (0.53, 0.85)$. Eigenvalues describe directions that keep their line. Singular values describe the longest and shortest stretch, and here they are 1.618 and 0.618.

screens.prose: You found input directions with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$. Together they give the **singular value decomposition** $$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^T$$ Here $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ are orthogonal, and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is diagonal with $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge 0$. Every matrix has one, square or not.
screens.question: Which line is the SVD of $\mathbf{A}$?

options.why: You dropped the transpose. The rows of $\mathbf{V}^T$ are the $\mathbf{v}_i$, so $\mathbf{V}^T\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 0)$ puts $\mathbf{v}_1$ on the axis.
You swapped the roles. $\mathbf{V}$ holds the input directions and acts first; $\mathbf{U}$ holds the output directions.
$\mathbf{U}^T$ would turn the axes away from the ellipse. The last turn must carry the axes onto $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$.

feedback.correct: Turn, stretch, turn: the matrix next to $\mathbf{x}$ acts first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the product from right to left: turn, stretch, turn.

byKey.noT: You dropped the transpose. $\mathbf{V}^T$, not $\mathbf{V}$, turns $\mathbf{v}_1$ onto the axis.

explain.text: Read right to left: $\mathbf{V}^T$ turns $\mathbf{v}_i$ onto the axes, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ stretches by $\sigma_i$, $\mathbf{U}$ turns the axes onto $\mathbf{u}_i$. Multiply the three matrices on the canvas and you get back $\mathbf{A}$.

screens.prose: Now show the factorisation follows from $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$. Let $\mathbf{V}$ have columns $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2$ and $\mathbf{U}$ have columns $\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_1 = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_2 = \sigma_2\mathbf{u}_2$: what the stages do to each direction
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$: put the two equations side by side as columns
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^T$: multiply both sides on the right by $\mathbf{V}^T$
$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^T$: the columns of $\mathbf{V}$ are orthonormal, so $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T = \mathbf{I}$

hints.text: Start from the fact about single directions.
Column $i$ of $\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is $\sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$.
Stack the two equations into $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, then undo $\mathbf{V}$ with $\mathbf{V}^T$.

feedback.correct: Each line follows from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with single directions, then stack, then remove $\mathbf{V}$.

byKey.done: $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T = \mathbf{I}$ can only be used once $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T$ appears. Multiply by $\mathbf{V}^T$ first.
byKey.mult: You need $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ before you can multiply it by $\mathbf{V}^T$.

explain.text: Stacking turns two vector equations into one matrix equation. Multiplying by $\mathbf{V}^T$ and using $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^T = \mathbf{I}$ isolates $\mathbf{A}$. Nothing here needed $\mathbf{A}$ to be symmetric or square.

screens.title: When the SVD is nothing new
screens.prose: $\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric positive definite, so $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^T$. Its eigenvalues are 3 and 1, along $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(-1,1)/\sqrt2$.
screens.question: What is the SVD of $\mathbf{S}$?

options.why: You took square roots of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{S}$. The roots come from $\mathbf{S}^T\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{S}^2$, whose eigenvalues are 9 and 1. Their roots are 3 and 1 again.
With $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}$ the stretch would act along the plain axes. Here the stretch acts along the eigenvectors, so $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{Q}$ too.

options.text: It has no SVD; it already has an eigendecomposition
options.why: Every matrix has an SVD. For this one it simply coincides with the eigendecomposition.

hints.text: Which directions does $\mathbf{S}$ stretch most and least?
The ellipse's axes lie along the eigenvectors.
$\mathbf{S}$ turns nothing: it stretches along $\mathbf{q}_1$ by 3 and along $\mathbf{q}_2$ by 1. So $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U} = \mathbf{Q}$.

feedback.correct: For a symmetric positive definite matrix the two decompositions agree.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which directions are stretched and by how much.

explain.text: The ellipse's axes are the eigenvectors, with lengths 3 and 1. So $\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{u}_i = \mathbf{q}_i$ and $\sigma_i = \lambda_i$. With a negative eigenvalue the sign moves into $\mathbf{U}$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 3 and −1 but singular values 3 and 1.

screens.title: The biggest combined move
screens.prose: Two desks face a rates shock $r$ and an equity shock $q$, in standard deviations. Desk 1 makes $2r + 2q$ and desk 2 makes $-r + q$, in £k. A risk manager tries every shock with $r^2 + q^2 = 1$. She looks for the shock that moves the desks' P&L furthest, by the length of the P&L vector.

state.caption: Dashed: the shocks with $r^2 + q^2 = 1$. Solid: the P&L each one gives.

screens.question: What is the largest length of the P&L vector, in £k?

hints.text: The P&L matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The answer is its largest singular value.
Its $\mathbf{M}^T\mathbf{M}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues 8 and 2.
$\sigma_1 = \sqrt{8} = 2.83$, from the shock $(r, q) = (0.71, 0.71)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the largest singular value of the P&L matrix.

byKey.both: You moved both factors by a full unit. That shock has length $\sqrt2$, more than the manager allows.
byKey.onefactor: $\sqrt5 = 2.24$ is one factor at a time. Moving both together, $(0.71, 0.71)$, moves the P&L further.
byKey.noroot: 8 is an eigenvalue of $\mathbf{M}^T\mathbf{M}$, a squared length. Take its square root.

explain.text: The largest move comes from $\mathbf{v}_1 = (0.71, 0.71)$, rates and equity moving together: P&L $(2.83, 0)$. The opposite shock, $-\mathbf{v}_1$, gives $(-2.83, 0)$, a £2.83k loss for desk 1. This matrix has no real eigenvalues at all, yet its SVD still finds the biggest move.

ideas: Any matrix sends the unit circle to an ellipse; the semi-axes have lengths $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2$, the singular values.
$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^T$: turn by $\mathbf{V}^T$, stretch by $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, turn by $\mathbf{U}$, so $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i\mathbf{u}_i$.
$\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$ for the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$; every matrix has an SVD, square or not.

formula.name: Singular value decomposition
formula.note: Read right to left: turn, stretch, turn.

summary.trap: Eigenvalues are not singular values: a shear has eigenvalues 1 and 1 but stretches by 1.618.

quiz.prose: A $2 \times 2$ matrix $\mathbf{A}$ has $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ with eigenvalues 25 and 4.
quiz.question: What is $\sigma_1$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

byKey.noroot: 25 is a squared stretch. Take its square root.
byKey.small: 2 is $\sigma_2$, the smaller one. $\sigma_1$ is the largest.

quiz.question: What are the singular values of $\mathbf{D}$?

options.why: Singular values are lengths of stretches, so they are never negative. The minus sign goes into $\mathbf{U}$.
Those are the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{D}^T\mathbf{D}$. Take square roots.

feedback.correct: 4 and 2: the sign is a flip, not a stretch.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how much each axis is stretched, ignoring flips.

quiz.prose: The shear $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 1 and 1. Its $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 5.83 and 0.17.
quiz.question: What is its largest singular value, to two decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of the larger eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

byKey.eig: 1 is an eigenvalue of the shear. It says nothing about the longest stretch.
byKey.noroot: 5.83 is a squared stretch. Take its square root.

explain.text: $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{3 + 2\sqrt2} = 1 + \sqrt2 \approx 2.41$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt2 - 1 \approx 0.41$. Their product is 1, the determinant.

options.why: $\mathbf{u}_2$ is an output direction. The input that lands there is $\mathbf{v}_2$.
$(0, 1)$ is where $\mathbf{V}^T$ sends $\mathbf{v}_2$, halfway through. $\mathbf{A}$ itself starts from $\mathbf{v}_2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow an input through turn, stretch, turn.

explain.text: $\mathbf{V}^T\mathbf{v}_2 = (0, 1)$, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ makes it $(0, \sigma_2)$, and $\mathbf{U}$ turns that to $\sigma_2\mathbf{u}_2$.
